Q201.L1t: Dehydration is a disturbance of fluid balance in which the body has lost more water, or water and salts, than it has taken in.
Q201.L2t: Hypernatraemia means a raised serum sodium concentration, and it is classified as a type of dehydration by the level of sodium in the blood.
Q201.L3t: In hypernatraemic dehydration the sodium concentration in the blood is high because the body has too little water relative to its sodium, which happens when the water taken in is not enough to replace the water lost.
Q201.L4t: Hypernatraemic dehydration is a state in which the water taken in is less than the body needs to stay in balance.
Q201.L2f: Hypernatraemic dehydration is diagnosed by a fall in serum sodium below the normal range of about 135 to 145 mmol/L.
Q201.L3f: Hypernatraemic dehydration arises when a person takes in excess water, which dilutes the body's sodium and so produces the raised sodium reading.
Q201.L4f: Hypernatraemic dehydration is a state in which the water taken in is greater than the body needs to stay in balance.

Q202.L1t: A peak flow meter is a hand-held device that measures the fastest speed at which a person can blow air out of the lungs.
Q202.L2t: Peak flow readings are normally taken as the best of three attempts, and the patient should use the same meter each time so that results can be compared.
Q202.L3t: Peak expiratory flow depends on how fully the chest and diaphragm can expand, and an upright posture gives the least restricted lung expansion, so readings are higher and more reproducible from one test to the next.
Q202.L4t: The patient should be upright because this allows the lungs to expand fully and gives readings that are accurate and consistent.
Q202.L2f: Peak flow meters should be calibrated by the patient before each reading, using a weight placed on the mouthpiece.
Q202.L3f: The main reason for the upright posture is practical rather than physiological: it puts the patient's mouth and chest in full view so that the clinician can watch each blow and check the technique, and lung expansion is largely unaffected by position.
Q202.L4f: The patient should be upright so that their technique can be easily observed by the person carrying out the test.

Q203.L1t: Intravenous therapy can lead to several local complications at the cannula site, and nurses are expected to check the site regularly for them.
Q203.L2t: Vesicant drugs, such as some chemotherapy agents, can destroy tissue when they escape from the vein, so they need especially careful administration and monitoring.
Q203.L3t: Of the terms listed, the one that specifically means leakage of a vesicant or irritant drug into the tissues around the vein is the one used when the damaging substance is a vesicant, whereas the terms for non-vesicant fluid leakage, for vein irritation and for a general tissue response do not carry this specific meaning.
Q203.L4t: The complication described is extravasation, which is the leakage of a vesicant medication into the surrounding tissues.
Q203.L2f: Complications at an IV site are rare because vesicant drugs are always given through large central veins, so they cannot leak into surrounding tissue.
Q203.L3f: The description refers to a general tissue response to irritation or injury, with redness, heat, swelling and pain at the site, and this response is the one that occurs when a vesicant drug leaks out, rather than a specific type of leakage.
Q203.L4f: The complication described is inflammation, which is the term for leakage of a vesicant medication into the surrounding tissues.
